HI-2026-GM1320.s: The governor signed this measure into law as Act 218. It requires health insurance and health plan contracts issued or renewed in Hawaii after December 31, 2026, to cover standard fertility preservation services for people who may have infertility from certain medically needed treatments, such as cancer treatment. It also bars insurers and plans from denying that coverage based on a prior diagnosis, past fertility treatment, or certain health factors.

HI-2026-GM1321.s: The law sets up state-funded help for colorectal cancer screenings and, for uninsured residents who need it after a screening, treatment too. It also says some health plans must cover these screenings and follow-up colonoscopies without deductibles or other cost sharing. The state will spend $1,800,000 for fiscal year 2026-2027 to run the program, and it takes effect on July 1, 2026.

HI-2026-GM1322.s: Act 220 was signed into law on July 9, 2026. It lets the state office of wellness and resilience run a program to buy and forgive medical debt for Hawaii residents who meet set income rules, subject to available funds. The program may use state, private, or federal money, and it must keep personal health and identity info private.

HI-2026-GM1323.s: The measure became law as Act 221 and changes hospital licensing rules in Hawaii. It tells the health department to let hospitals use accreditation or certification from any organization approved by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to show they meet state licensing inspection rules. It also lets the department keep doing inspections or checks for complaints, bad findings, or regular review, and makes the related reports and letters public.

HI-2026-GM1324.s: Signed into law, this measure requires all licensed hospitals with emergency departments to report de-identified syndromic surveillance data to the state health department. That data can include chief complaints, diagnoses, visit dates, patient demographics, ZIP code, and facility location. The health department may also set up a state reporting system and add more reporting rules for other entities.

HI-2026-GM1325.s: Signed into law on July 9, 2026, this measure requires the state health planning and development agency to make a state plan on hearing loss. The plan must review hearing loss data, screening, access to care, training, and ways to improve services and awareness. It also sets a first report due before the 2027 regular session and provides $100,000 for fiscal year 2026-2027 to help develop and publish the plan.

HI-2026-GM1327.s: The governor signed this measure into law as Act 225. It changes Hawaii law on bribery and sets a nine-year time limit to start a bribery case. It also says someone convicted of bribery cannot use a deferred plea deal.

HI-2026-GM1329.s: On July 10, 2026, the governor signed this measure into law as Act 227. It changes campaign finance rules so candidate committees and noncandidate committees must file several reports, forms, loan documents, and fundraiser notices electronically with the Campaign Spending Commission. It also adds an electronic filing step for candidates who want public campaign funds.

HI-2026-GM1330.s: Signed into law as Act 228, the measure bars certain top Hawaii executive branch employees from going to political fundraisers or asking for campaign donations. It applies to employees appointed by the governor to paid jobs that need Senate confirmation, while they hold that covered job. The law says they may still vote, make personal political donations, and share political views as private people.

HI-2026-GM1333.s: The law lets licensed mental health counselors be appointed as child custody evaluators in Hawaii. These evaluators help family courts decide custody cases, and the change affects families going through those cases and the professionals who can do the work. It took effect when the governor approved it on July 10, 2026.

HI-2026-GM1334.s: The governor signed this measure into law as Act 232 on July 10, 2026. It deals with state bonds and includes findings about Hawaii’s debt limit. The act lists past and estimated net general fund revenue and bond debt figures used to check that limit.

HI-2026-GM1336.s: Signed into law on July 13, 2026, this act would add new protections for Department of Education and state public charter school workers, including sports officials. It would require schools to have steps for reporting and handling harassment, make yearly safety training, and create written safety plans for harmful situations. It would also allow paid leave for court dates tied to harassment cases and let the attorney general help workers seek a temporary restraining order, with some reimbursement for serving papers but not lawyer or court fees.

HI-2026-GM1342.s: Signed into law on July 13, 2026, this act lets the state education department create a program to give high school diplomas to some people who did not finish school because they were inducted into the U.S. armed services or because wartime events interrupted their schooling. It applies to people affected during World War II, the Korean War, or the Vietnam War. People would need to show they qualify using forms set by the department.

HI-2026-GM1343.s: The law changes Hawaii’s school impact fee rules for housing projects. It expands exemptions for certain homes, including projects with fewer than 500 units, some affordable units, and small studio units, and it sets new timing rules for land dedication or fee-in-lieu agreements for projects with 100 or more units. It also repeals a sunset and reporting rule, restructures some school fee accounts, and keeps existing education contribution agreements in place.

HI-2026-GM1344.s: The governor signed this education bill into law as Act 242 on July 13, 2026. Starting with the 2028-2029 school year, Hawaii Department of Education schools must give approved dyslexia-aware reading screenings to students in kindergarten through grade 3 and to new students entering a school for the first time in the state. Schools must also provide evidence-based help for students flagged with dyslexia or reading problems, and the department must offer teacher training in structured reading instruction and work with teacher training programs.

HI-2026-GM1345.s: The measure became Act 243 and is called the Hawaii Braille Literacy Education Act. It requires the state education department to provide braille instruction and braille learning materials for eligible students with low vision or blindness when certain conditions are met. It also sets out braille literacy support services, information sharing with the human services department, and work on section 504 plans and individualized education programs.

HI-2026-GM1349.s: Signed into law on July 14, 2026, this act sets rules for AI-made fake images, audio, or video that look like a real person. It makes it unlawful to publish a realistic digital imitation of an identifiable person without consent if it is used in ads, causes harm, or is used for fraud, defamation, harassment, or other crimes. It also gives people a way to seek civil remedies, and it does not apply to parody, satire, commentary, criticism, scholarship, political or educational expression, news reporting, or some documentary or historical uses.

HI-2026-GM1355.s: Signed into law on July 14, 2026, this act limits when operators of smart household security devices may share user data with law enforcement. Sharing is allowed only with written user consent, a court warrant, or in a narrow emergency, and operators cannot make consent a condition of using the device. It also lets the attorney general take action for violations and treats violations as unfair or deceptive business practices.

HI-2026-GM1356.s: The law says businesses in Hawaii must clearly show the total price when they advertise, display, or offer live-event tickets or short-term lodging, like hotels and vacation rentals. It also requires them to clearly explain extra fees before a customer agrees to pay, and bars them from hiding or misstating those fees. Offers that follow the federal rule on these prices are treated as meeting this state law.

HI-2026-GM1357.s: On July 14, 2026, the governor signed this insurance bill into law as Act 255. It changes when the insurance commissioner must examine captive insurance companies, including a new schedule for risk retention captive insurance companies. It also asks for a report to the legislature in 2031 on how the new exam rules are working.

HI-2026-GM1360.s: The governor returned SB 2600 with a line-item veto, which means he reduced one specific money item in the bill. The $50 million general fund deposit to the Emergency and Budget Reserve Fund was cut to $1. It affects the state budget and the fund that serves as a reserve for emergencies or budget shortfalls.

HI-2026-GM1361.s: The bill became Act 258 and requires the Department of Transportation to set rules for a clean fuel standard in Hawaii by January 1, 2028. The rules must phase in lower carbon fuel standards, with diesel and gasoline starting on January 1, 2029, and use a method for measuring greenhouse gas emissions across a fuel’s full life cycle. It affects fuel producers and users in the state, and the standards are meant to cut emissions from transportation fuels.

HI-2026-GM1362.s: Signed into law on July 15, 2026, this act updates Hawaii rules for electric bicycles, mopeds, and electric motorcycles. It sets safe riding rules for e-bikes, bars high-speed electric devices from public roads and paths, and says road-legal electric bicycles do not need insurance. It also requires labels, warning signs, and buyer info for electric bikes, and it bans mopeds and electric motorcycles from bike lanes and bike paths.

HI-2026-GM1364.s: The bill became Act 261 and was signed into law on July 15, 2026. It lets a deaf motor vehicle owner ask for a deafness mark on the vehicle registration, using the international symbol for deafness or a code. That mark would show up when law enforcement checks the vehicle record so officers are alerted that the owner is deaf. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027.

HI-2026-GM1365.s: On July 15, 2026, the governor signed this traffic safety law. It gives the Department of Transportation $2 million in fiscal year 2026-2027 to add pedestrian safety improvements near school property, with other sites also possible. The work can include all-way crosswalks, raised intersections, and similar safety measures.

HI-2026-GM1366.s: Signed into law on July 15, 2026, this act changes pay rules for some Hawaii housing agencies. It lets the Hawaii Housing Finance and Development Corporation and the Hawaii Community Development Authority set certain staff roles and salaries with fewer review steps, and it raises salary caps for the top leaders and one deputy role. It also sets rules for employment contracts at HHFDC, HCDA, and the Hawaii Public Housing Authority.

HI-2026-GM1368.s: The law puts $50 million from state general revenue into Hawaii’s emergency and budget reserve fund. It is meant to help the state during an emergency, economic downturn, or other drop in revenue. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

HI-2026-GM1369.s: On July 15, 2026, the governor returned SB 3262 without approval. The bill would have changed how the Hawaiʻi Teacher Standards Board picks its executive director, using a list of three nominees and Senate advice and consent. It affects the Board of Education and the Hawaiʻi Teacher Standards Board.

HI-2026-GM1370.s: The measure became law on July 16, 2026, as Act 266. It creates a three-year pilot program in Kauai and Hawaii counties that would let certain licensed clinical psychologists, under a doctor or psychiatrist’s supervision, prescribe some mental health medicines to patients ages 18 to 65 at federally qualified health centers. The state health planning and development agency would report back to lawmakers on whether to expand, make permanent, or end the program.

HI-2026-GM817.s: The governor informed the Senate that Danielle M. Bass was appointed to temporarily serve as the senator for Senate District 18, which includes Waipi'o, Crestview, Royal Kunia, part of Mililani, part of Waipahu, and part of Akupu. Her service began at once. The appointment fills the vacancy left by Senator Michelle N. Kidani’s resignation and will end on November 3, 2026.

HI-2026-HB1713.s: The law changes school impact fees for some housing projects. It expands who can be exempt, sets clearer steps and timing for land dedication or fee-in-lieu deals for new homes, and keeps existing education contribution deals in place. It also changes how some school impact fee accounts are set up and ends the sunset and reporting rules from a 2025 act.

HI-2026-HB1753.s: Hawaii law now requires certain social media sites to give users a clear way to delete their accounts and erase personal and sensitive personal information tied to those accounts. It also bars deceptive practices that block account deletion. The Attorney General may bring civil cases and seek court orders and penalties for violations. It takes effect on 7/1/2027.

HI-2026-HB1785.s: The law lets the Superintendent hire a new contractor if a student bus contractor misses service for five or more straight school days. It also lets the Department of Education charge a penalty when a contractor misses a service segment without an approved reason. The School Bus Fare Revolving Fund may be used to help pay for replacement service.

HI-2026-HB1804.s: Requires the Executive Office on Aging to set up a study on ways to pay for long-term care services, including public and private options, and to report the findings to the Legislature. It also lets the office hire the University of Hawaii to help with the study and provides money for it. The bill became law as Act 249.

HI-2026-HB1853.s: Creates the Hanai Memory Network Program in the Executive Office on Aging. The program would build a network of dementia care specialists and support services to help people with dementia and their caregivers. It also provides money for the program.

HI-2026-HB1864.s: For insurance policies, contracts, plans, and agreements issued or renewed after 12/31/2026, health insurers, mutual benefit societies, and health maintenance organizations must cover standard fertility preservation services for people getting medically needed treatment that may cause infertility. The rule applies to people whose treatment could cause infertility because of the treatment itself. The bill became law as Act 218.

HI-2026-HB1888.s: The law requires the state education department and public charter schools to take steps to better address harassment of educational workers, including sports officials. It lets the Attorney General help these workers get a temporary restraining order if they face harassment or intentional bodily injury at school sports events. It also makes some harassment of educational workers, and disruption of school functions or school board work, a misdemeanor.

HI-2026-HB1890.s: The law provides annual salary step increases for public school and public charter school teachers who have completed one year of satisfactory service and meet other set requirements. The raises would apply only if included in a union contract and if the Legislature funds them. It became Act 233 in 2026.

HI-2026-HB1891.s: The law requires the Department of Education to use dyslexia-friendly school screenings and proven help for students who need it. It also calls for teacher training in structured literacy, which is a step-by-step way to teach reading, and support for teacher prep programs to teach that method. It became Act 242 in 2026.

HI-2026-HB1969.s: The law requires Hawaii’s Human Services Department to create a state-funded program for colorectal cancer screenings and treatment for certain people. It also requires coverage for follow-up care, including a colonoscopy after a positive test, with no deductible, copay, coinsurance, or other cost share. The law also provides funding and adds one full-time staff position.

HI-2026-HB1973.s: Creates a one-year KupunAloha pilot program in the Department of Health to give in-home health care and support services to people who qualify for the program but do not already get government help for these services. It also sets aside money for the pilot program. The program sunsets on 6/30/2027.

HI-2026-HB1974.s: Creates and funds a state hearing loss plan for the State Health Planning and Development Agency to develop and publish. It affects the agency and state health planning work. It became law as Act 223 in 2026.

HI-2026-HB2021.s: This law sets rules for electric bicycles, high-speed electric devices, mopeds, electric motorcycles, and electric micro-mobility devices. It bars electric bicycles from unsafe riding and requires labels, signs, and written disclosures about electric bicycle laws. It also limits where certain devices can be used, requires registration for electric bicycles, and sets helmet, age, and supervision rules for some riders.

HI-2026-HB2023.s: Hawaii passed a law that sets up a statewide program to certify active intelligent speed assistance systems and choose a vendor to install and maintain them. It also limits civil liability for car makers, distributors, and sellers tied to these systems, and makes tampering with one a misdemeanor. Courts may order these systems for some repeat traffic offenders, and the law takes effect on January 1, 2028.

HI-2026-HB2137.s: Creates rules against some harmful uses of realistic digital copies made by artificial intelligence. It also sets out exceptions and lets people who are harmed sue for civil remedies, which are court-ordered fixes or money awards. The law affects people and groups that make or use these AI-made digital imitations in Hawaii.

HI-2026-HB2296.s: Hawaii law requires the Department of Education to charge at least one-quarter of the cost to prepare each school meal. It affects school meal prices in public schools. The measure became Act 236 on July 13, 2026.

HI-2026-HB2338.s: This law changes the Hawaii Community College Promise Program for students at University of Hawaii community colleges. It removes grants, scholarships, and other funding sources from the award calculation, and it lets students apply those funds toward indirect costs like housing, food, and other living expenses. It also allows the program to coordinate with federal student aid programs to maximize total financial assistance available to students.

HI-2026-HB2344.s: Creates a short-term, independent commission to study Hawaii public schools and make a plan for school consolidations, realignments, and closures. The commission would report to the Legislature, and lawmakers would use an expedited process to review the plan. The bill also provides money for this work and became law as Act 264 in 2026.

HI-2026-HB2452.s: Becomes law and lets the state issue general obligation bonds, which are state loans paid back over time. It also says the required findings have been made that the bonds will not push the state over its debt limit. This affects state borrowing and the state budget.

HI-2026-SB2031.s: The bill became law and requires businesses to clearly show the total price when they advertise live-event tickets or short-term lodging. It also bars them from misreporting fees or charges in those offers or ads. Ads or offers that follow the federal rule on unfair or deceptive fees are treated as meeting this state law.

HI-2026-SB2043.s: The law changes how often certain captive insurance companies are checked by the Insurance Commissioner. Before 12/31/2031, they must be examined no later than five years after licensing, and the commissioner may do more exams if needed. Starting on 1/1/2032, they must be examined at least once every five years, and the commissioner must send a report to the Legislature before the 2031 Regular Session. Effective 7/1/2026.

HI-2026-SB2259.s: Creates the Hawaii Dementia Initiative Business Recognition Program within the Department of Business, Economic Development, and Tourism. It also sets aside money for the program. The bill became law as Act 251 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB2271.s: The law lets the Department of Health make rules so hospitals can show they meet state license checks through approved outside accreditation or certification. The outside group must be approved by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. It became Act 221 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB2338.s: This law changes hiring and pay rules for the Hawaii Housing Finance and Development Corporation, the Hawaii Community Development Authority, and the Hawaii Public Housing Authority. It gives HHFDC and HCDA more control over certain personnel actions and job descriptions, and it changes the title of HHFDC’s Executive Assistant to Deputy Executive Director. It also changes salary limits for the executive directors and deputy executive director, and sets conditions for employment contracts issued by these agencies.

HI-2026-SB2494.s: Creates a nine-year time limit for bringing a bribery case. It affects bribery cases in Hawaii and became law as Act 225 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB2532.s: The bill would require certain campaign finance forms to be filed online through the Campaign Spending Commission’s updated electronic filing system. It affects people and groups covered by Hawaii’s campaign spending laws and took effect on 11/4/2026.

HI-2026-SB2568.s: The law makes harassment a misdemeanor when it is aimed at a public servant because of their job or while they are doing official duties. It applies to people who work as public servants and became Act 237 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB2600.s: The bill became Act 265 and makes a deposit from state money into the emergency and budget reserve fund, which is the state savings fund. It affects the state’s general fund and the reserve fund used for emergencies and budget shortfalls.

HI-2026-SB2614.s: Allows Hawaii’s education department to give a high school diploma to some people who never got one because they entered or served in the U.S. armed forces, or because war-related events interrupted their schooling during World War II, the Korean War, or the Vietnam War. It applies to people who qualify under those rules. The bill became law as Act 240 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB2851.s: The law lets deaf vehicle owners register their car so a deafness note shows when police look up the vehicle. It takes effect on 1/1/2027 and applies to deaf drivers in Hawaii.

HI-2026-SB2852.s: Became law as Act 257 on July 14, 2026. It requires the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission to make rules on digital access for public places, in line with certain federal rules. It also treats it as unlawful discrimination to deny a person with a disability full and equal use of goods, services, facilities, or information by using technology they cannot access.

HI-2026-SB2877.s: The law requires the Department of Education to create a two-year pilot program where students write and publish books. It may run for fourth, fifth, and sixth graders at up to five public elementary schools in Kalihi and up to five in Nanakuli-Waianae, and it must fit into regular class work. It also sets aside money for the program.

HI-2026-SB2964.s: Passed law on July 14, 2026, with an effective date of January 1, 2027. It requires homeowners insurance agents to tell policyholders they may send in info about upgrades to their home, and those details must be sent to the insurer. Insurers must then review the home's replacement cost estimate and offer more coverage if needed. It also sets administrative penalties for violations.

HI-2026-SB2999.s: The law requires Hawaii's Department of Transportation to make rules by January 1, 2028 for a clean fuel standard for alternative fuels in the state. It also requires reports and public information sessions. It became Act 258 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB3001.s: Requires people who run AI companions in Hawaii to give users certain notices and to set up steps for prompts about suicidal thoughts or self-harm. It also adds protections for users, including minors, and starts yearly reports to the Health Department on 1/1/2028. Breaking these rules can be treated as an unfair or deceptive business practice.

HI-2026-SB3025.s: Creates a program in the Office of Wellness and Resilience to buy and forgive unpaid medical debt for Hawaii residents, if program funds are available. It also requires a report to the Legislature. The law includes money for the program.

HI-2026-SB3118.s: The bill updates references to the U.S. Code in the Interstate Compact on Educational Opportunity for Military Children. It affects the state rules used for school matters for children of military families. It became law as Act 239 on July 13, 2026.

HI-2026-SB3132.s: Hospitals in Hawaii with emergency departments would have to send syndromic surveillance data, which is health data used to spot disease patterns, to the Department of Health. The department could set up a statewide system to collect and report that data. It became law as Act 222 in 2026.

HI-2026-SB3234.s: Becomes law and gives money to the Department of Transportation to install pedestrian safety improvements near school properties. It also allows other sites to be considered for these upgrades.

HI-2026-SB3253.s: The law recognizes the Hawaii Conservation Sanctuary as a nonprofit group created under a 2026 Senate resolution. It is meant to protect and grow populations of endangered species and other wildlife in Hawaii.

HI-2026-SB3262.s: The bill would change how the Hawaii Teacher Standards Board picks its Executive Director. It would require the board to send three names to the Board of Education, which would choose one from that list, with Senate advice and consent. The bill was vetoed.

HI-2026-SB847.s: The law sets up a three-year pilot program in Kauai County and Hawaii County. It lets qualified psychologists, while under a supervising physician or psychiatrist, prescribe certain mental health medicines to patients ages 18 to 65 who are under their care. It also tells the Board of Psychology to make rules and the State Health Planning and Development Agency to report to the Legislature.
